doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Cabaret cards, arrest and ninety days in jail
summary: Police enforce cabaret cards after Sinatra's protest and arrest Ware for the bass; he serves 90 days.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And, at that particular time, Frank Sinatra, as well as Sophie Tucker refused to work in New York in those big rooms unless they abolished that cabaret card business. And that made the police department mad, and they started going around raiding the clubs, and whoever had any kind of minor bust, you know, they were snatching their cards from them.

So naturally we had to look out for everything, so "I'll meet you in the morning, Jimmy says to me, we're gonna go down in the morning to get your cabaret card straightened out, you know, and reissue it to you because it had elapsed, and he said, "Yeah man, I got a Buell fiddle that you can have" -- and give me a bass. And he ended Allen Eager had given up getting me an apartment, and I was living there right on

West Broadway, and next morning, Jimmy comes by dutifully, and we go down to the license bureau, and sitting up there, the man says, "Oh yeah, Wilbur Ware -- have a seat." He says to me, "We'll get your card straightened out for you in a few minutes." So I'm sitting and sitting, and Jimmy said, "Well, what's the trouble?" and he says, "Oh, we're getting to it" and pretty soon here come two detectives. They called out to Brooklyn. And the come in and said, "Oh, here's that bass fiddle snatcher we been looking for." All because of Sinatra, or anything they can do to harass, you know, so naturally I didn't get the job; they carted me out to the jail out there in Brooklyn.

And they were really picking on us, and Peck said, "Man, I don't want to see the man in jail, and he said, 'I've seen Wilbur, and I did see him out in Chicago -- he came out there to play a concert.' One of those jazz festivals, you know? And he asked me when I was gonna pay him his money and I said as soon as I start making some money, and he said, okay. Well, I squared it with him ... but the police wanted to make a big thing out of it, and he said 'I don't want to prosecute him', and he told them, "He's gonna pay me back'.
But the police said to him, "Oh, we can't do that; we did a whole lot of work on this case' -- a whole lot of BS!
And so I had laid up there in that jail

for almost 90 days. It's time I go to court, and he's telling the judge that he didn't want to prosecute me or nothing, and the judge said, 'No, he's got to plead guilty to something.' In other words, I had to cop out. So finally I said okay. He says, 'Well, you have 5 more days here.' 'How long you been in already?' and I say, '85 days', and he says, 'Well, you got to do 90 days, and that 5 more days must be served', and so I had to lay in jail for five more days!
